title: Collaborative Filtering & Matrix Factorization
summary: Learn from the crowd instead of item features — the user-item matrix, neighborhood methods, and matrix factorization, the still most-asked recommender technique.

slides.markdown:
Collaborative filtering starts from one data structure: the **user-item interaction matrix**, rows are users, columns are items, and each cell is a rating or an implicit signal (watched, clicked, bought). Most cells are empty — that's the whole problem to solve.

The core bet of collaborative filtering: if you can spot patterns across *this matrix alone* — no item features, no user demographics — you can predict the missing cells. "Users who rated similarly on the items they've both seen tend to agree on the ones they haven't" is the entire idea.

The earliest collaborative filtering methods are **neighborhood-based**:

- **User-based CF** — find users similar to you (by overlapping ratings), then recommend what they liked that you haven't seen.
- **Item-based CF** — find items similar to an item you liked (by co-rating patterns across all users), then recommend those. Amazon's original "customers who bought this also bought" is item-based CF.

Item-based CF tends to be more stable in production because item-item similarity changes slowly, while a user's neighborhood of similar users can shift session to session.

**Matrix factorization** replaces explicit neighborhoods with learned **latent vectors**. Every user gets a vector `p_u`, every item gets a vector `q_i`, both in the same low-dimensional space (say, 50 dimensions), and the predicted rating is just their dot product: `r̂_ui = p_u · q_i`.

Those latent dimensions aren't hand-designed — they're learned by minimizing prediction error on the ratings you *do* have (typically with gradient descent plus L2 regularization). A dimension might end up correlating with "how much action vs romance" without anyone ever labeling it that way — the model discovers whatever structure best explains the observed ratings.

slides.subTitle: Decomposing the interaction matrix
slides.markdown:
The picture worth keeping: an `m×n` ratings matrix `R` is approximated as the product of an `m×k` user-factor matrix `P` and a `k×n` item-factor matrix `Qᵀ`, where `k` (say 50–200) is far smaller than `m` or `n`.

![Interaction matrix decomposed into user and item factor matrices](assets/matrix-factorization.svg)

Every row of `P` is one user's latent taste vector; every column of `Qᵀ` is one item's latent vector. Multiplying a user row by an item column reconstructs a predicted rating for every cell — including the ones that were originally empty, which is exactly the prediction you wanted.

assets.alt: Interaction matrix decomposed into user and item factor matrices

slides.markdown:
Most real data is implicit (clicks, watches), not explicit ratings — and implicit feedback has no negatives. A user who never watched something might dislike it, or might simply not have seen it yet; you can't tell.

Implicit-feedback matrix factorization (e.g. the classic **weighted ALS** approach) handles this by treating every unobserved interaction as a weak negative and every observed one as a strong positive, then weighting the loss by *confidence* — a video watched 10 times is a far more confident positive than one watched once. This reframes the objective from "predict the rating" to "predict the confidence that this user prefers this item."

The interaction matrix is almost entirely empty — a streaming service with 10,000 titles and a user who's watched 40 has seen 0.4% of the catalog, and that's typical, not extreme. Naive approaches (like computing raw user-user correlation) fall apart here: two users who happen to share only 2 ratings can look artificially "identical" or wildly dissimilar from pure noise.

Matrix factorization handles sparsity better than neighborhood methods because it doesn't need users to overlap directly — two users can be similar through a *chain* of shared latent structure even if they've never rated a single common item.

The clean, non-technical explanation: imagine describing every user and every movie using the same handful of "taste dimensions" (how much action, how much romance, how arthouse) — except you never write those dimensions down by hand, you let the algorithm infer them purely from who rated what.

Once every user and every movie has a position in that same taste space, predicting a rating is just checking how well-aligned they are. That's matrix factorization in a sentence, and it's usually enough to satisfy a non-ML interviewer probing for understanding rather than derivation.
